transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-20 15:30 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Omar Valdez (Redwood SE), Maya Li (Aurum CTO), Jamal Ortiz (Aurum Platform), Lena Bauer (Aurum Security), Ethan Park (Aurum SRE)

[00:00] Alex Kim: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, short agenda: get through artifact transport options for air-gapped, offline license flow, and then go into runtime stress test plan. priya will walk through runtime tuning.
[00:18] Maya Li: great thanks, alex. quick context - we have a 6-node lab (4x A100 80GB + 2x A40 for inference dev), all firewalled, no egress. we're planning a pilot to run Redwood Private in sealed mode. need to validate bundle delivery and the licensing activation without internet.
[00:35] Priya Shah: got it. we'll cover the bundle format, signed manifests, and the offline license handshake. also want to talk about kernel modules for the nvdriver and the preferred kernel versions — we've seen folks on RHEL7/8 and Ubuntu 22.04 have different paths.
[00:52] Jamal Ortiz: important: we run custom distro images with a minimal footprint. we prefer not to change kernel versions frequently. can you do a runtime that supports the current images?
[01:10] Priya Shah: yes, we support a range but there are driver ABI constraints; if you keep to the list in the compatibility matrix we provide the signed driver modules will load without rebuilding. if you deviate we can either provide prebuilt dkms packages or a driver module you can insmod.
[01:28] Lena Bauer: how do you verify integrity of the artifact during air transfer? our compliance requires chain-of-custody logs and tamper-evidence.
[01:38] Alex Kim: good question. our recommended flow: we produce a signed bundle (PKCS7) with SHA-256 checksums per artifact, we include a manifest with serial numbers + sig, and we provide a USB transfer checklist + transfer log template for chain-of-custody. we'll also timestamp the manifest.
[01:58] Maya Li: is that signature verifiable offline?
[02:03] Omar Valdez: yes the public key is embedded in the installer image; verification is done locally with our verify tool, so no external CA calls are required.
[02:18] Ethan Park: what about licensing — we can't reach your licensing service from the lab. how does offline activation work?
[02:27] Priya Shah: we have two options: 1) One-time activation token: we issue a signed offline activation blob tied to the customer's HW fingerprint that you place in the appliance; validation is purely local. 2) Air-gap shuttle activation: you generate a CSR locally, we sign it, and hand back a license file that the runtime accepts. both methods require the signed manifest and checksum to be present.
[02:49] Jamal Ortiz: the HW fingerprint — is that MACs only or do you include GPU serials, disk serials?
[02:56] Priya Shah: we prefer combination: NIC MAC + primary disk serial + GPU unique id when available. that reduces risk if hardware is swapped.
[03:10] Maya Li: ok, later in the call we want to run a stress test to see steady-state throughput and tail latency. do you have a suggested workload?
[03:21] Priya Shah: yes — we usually run a 2-phase test: warmup with prefix caching (KV cache pre-populated) then sustained RPS ramp to target, measuring p50/p95/p99 and GPU util. we'll also simulate KV cache misses to understand cold-start token penalty.
[03:40] Alex Kim: one note — in air-gapped installs we've seen folks forget to enable persistent KV cache on the filesystem, which causes repeated cold K-V cache misses, so throughput tanks. check the runtime config for cache.persist=true.
[03:58] Jamal Ortiz: what's the recommended KV size? we have many models, some with long context; guessing 12GB per GPU is too much?
[04:07] Priya Shah: KV checkpoint size depends on model and kv cache policy; we recommend warmup partial prefixes for top-20 prompts and a 2-4GB persistent kv per GPU for most conversational models. for long-context LLMs you should plan 8-12GB if you want hot-cache for extended histories.
[04:30] Maya Li: and batching config — our use case is medium latency, high throughput. we can tolerate 50-100 ms extra tail if it halves token cost. what's your typical batch policy?
[04:42] Priya Shah: we use adaptive continuous batching: target latency SLO and max batch size. defaults are target 150ms, max batch 32 for 80b regs, but on A100 with sequence 1024 you can push higher batch sizes. we'll run tuning in the lab to find the cost/latency knee.
[05:00] Ethan Park: any caveat about quantization? we plan to test INT8 to reduce memory; does that change the runtime path?
[05:08] Priya Shah: yes quantization changes kernel selection; INT8 can reduce memory and sometimes reduce latency, but for some ops the INT8 kernels are slower on older drivers. we recommend quant-test A/B: one run with FP16, one with INT8 quantized model. also ensure your cuBLAS/cuDNN driver stack matches the kernel expectations.
[05:33] Maya Li: driver stack — we currently run driver 525.x on our images, is that supported?
[05:39] Omar Valdez: we certify 525.x and 535.x for our current runtime but some INT8 kernels use new cuBLAS primitives only in 535+. if you can upgrade to 535 in lab for the INT8 run that would be ideal. for strict compliance we can use a fallback kernel but it may penalize throughput.
[05:58] Jamal Ortiz: what about kernel module signing? if we have Secure Boot enabled we need signed kernel modules. can you provide signed modules?
[06:05] Priya Shah: yes we deliver signed .ko files when customers require Secure Boot. we'll include the public key for MokEnroll and documentation for efitools if you need to enroll.
[06:18] Lena Bauer: any telemetry — we can't ship data out, so what observability is available locally?
[06:25] Alex Kim: Redwood Private can run its observability stack entirely local; we write token-level metering to local DB and you can export compressed logs manually. we also support a local-only metrics UI with RBAC.
[06:38] Maya Li: ok let's get into the stress test plan. Priya?
[06:42] Priya Shah: plan: Phase 0 prep: verify installer image and checksums, confirm driver modules and license blob present. Phase 1: install and smoke test (model load latency, simple 1k token gen). Phase 2: KV warmup — run scripted prompts to populate persistent KV caches. Phase 3: ramp RPS from 10->200 over 30 minutes, measure p50/p95/p99 and GPU util. Phase 4: cold-start injection — simulate node restart to measure cache rebuild. Phase 5: INT8 quant run and compare. We'll provide a runbook with exact commands.
[07:18] Ethan Park: what's the expected GPU util for a steady 200 RPS on our A100 80GB with 70 token responses?
[07:26] Priya Shah: ballpark: for that config you may hit 70-85% util depending on prompt length and batching. we can tune batcher target to trade latency for util.
[07:38] Maya Li: what does the runtime log for KV hits look like? we want to be able to ingest a simple CSV of hit/miss by timestamp.
[07:46] Omar Valdez: runtime emits KV metrics per request: kv_hit=true/false, kv_latency_ms, model_tokens_served; we can output to local Prometheus with a compatible exporter; then you can query and dump CSV.
[08:00] Jamal Ortiz: one of our constraints is that the install media must be physically delivered via secure courier. how big are these bundles? can we split them?
[08:10] Alex Kim: bundles typically 4-40GB depending on model artifacts; for large models we support chunked bundles and an assembler tool that verifies chunk checksums and reassembles on-host. chunk size is configurable; we recommend 8GB chunks on USBs to match common sticks.
[08:29] Lena Bauer: what about fingerprinting the USB? we need to record serial and create audit log.
[08:34] Priya Shah: we include a transfer audit sheet where you note serial number of the media, timestamp, courier signature; our verify tool also logs the media serial when available.
[08:46] Maya Li: are there known gotchas with older NIC card firmwares? our BMCs are a bit old.
[08:54] Omar Valdez: older NICs with offload issues can cause jitter on large payload transfers; for bulk transfer we recommend using a dedicated transfer host with a modern NIC and then rsync the assembled artifacts locally. also disable TSO/GSO if you see corrupts.
[09:12] Jamal Ortiz: can you walk through a sample offline activation flow? step-by-step?
[09:17] Priya Shah: sure — step 1: you run redwoodctl generate-csr --hw-fingerprint > csr.bin. Step 2: export csr.bin and courier to Redwood signing team in a secure envelope, step 3: Redwood signs and returns license.license.bin. Step 4: run redwoodctl apply-license --file license.license.bin. Step 5: runtime validates sig and unlocks nodes. We'll provide a signed example and a template manifest.
[09:47] Maya Li: timeline — if we courier today, how fast do you turn around signing?
[09:52] Alex Kim: typical SLA for offline signing is 24 business hours once we receive the CSR in our secure CD. if you have an emergency we can expedite.
[10:01] Ethan Park: ok next, let's talk about kernel modules for the A100s — any special udev rules?
[10:07] Priya Shah: udev rules we provide ensure /dev/nv* device nodes persist and set modes. also we ship a small init hook to preload kernel params for hugepages and memlock. you should run sysctl profile we include.
[10:25] Jamal Ortiz: huge pages — do we need transparent hugepages off?
[10:29] Priya Shah: we recommend THP=never for stability with large sequence workloads; we'll document the exact sysctl and limits.conf entries.
[10:40] Maya Li: during the stress test can your team be on call to debug kernel oops or module load failures?
[10:46] Alex Kim: yes, Priya and Omar will be on call for the run window. we ask you to share jump host and log access beforehand.
[10:55] Lena Bauer: security question — are the signed drivers reproducible? do we provide source or just binaries?
[11:02] Omar Valdez: we provide binaries for the standard drivers; for customers requiring full SBOM and source we can provide source tarballs under NDA and build instructions. kernel module signing keys are Redwood-managed unless you supply your own signing key.
[11:20] Maya Li: we may want to sign modules with our key. is that supported?
[11:24] Priya Shah: yes, we can give you unsigned .ko and the signing instructions; you can sign them with your key and use MokEnroll to enroll. there is also an option to provide your public key so we sign with a customer-managed key in the bundle.
[11:40] Ethan Park: about performance monitoring — what metrics do you collect locally?
[11:46] Priya Shah: token latency, model mem usage, KV hit ratio, batch sizes per step, per-GPU util, PCIe transfer latency, and system counters. logs are gzipped and stored in /var/log/redwood.
[12:02] Jamal Ortiz: can we configure sampling rate? we don't want to fill disk during long runs.
[12:07] Priya Shah: yes sampling config and retention policies are adjustable; default is 1% traces and 10s metric scrape. we'll share recommended limits for the lab.
[12:22] Maya Li: let's cover the quantization plan. do you recommend per-layer calibration?
[12:28] Priya Shah: yes we use a calibration harness: pass a representative prompt set, collect activation statistics and generate a per-layer quant config. we also recommend validating output quality with our evals harness to catch regressions.
[12:44] Jamal Ortiz: any gotchas with INT8 on mixed-precision workloads?
[12:49] Priya Shah: watch out for operator fallback: some ops may fallback to FP16 introducing extra memcpy and slowdown. our profiler flags fallbacks and we can provide mitigations such as operator fusion or slightly different quant params.
[13:06] Maya Li: question from Lena — audit logs retention: can we lock tamper-evident logs locally?
[13:12] Alex Kim: yes we support append-only local audit logs with optional hardware-backed sealing if you have an HSM. for air-gapped we can sign logs with a local signing key and include a manifest for later verification.
[13:29] Lena Bauer: perfect. last parts: what do you need from us before the run?
[13:34] Priya Shah: we need: 1) inventory (NICs, GPU SKUs, kernel versions), 2) preferred transfer media type (USB/SSD), 3) courier schedule, 4) acceptance criteria for p95/p99.
[13:48] Jamal Ortiz: acceptance criteria: p95 < 300ms (for 70 token aver), p99 < 700ms for our interactive tier, and throughput > 150 RPS sustained across cluster.
[14:05] Alex Kim: we'll take that as the target. We'll run the warmup and then tune batching to meet cost/latency.
[14:12] Maya Li: any final comments on storage layout for persistent KV cache?
[14:16] Priya Shah: recommended: ext4/xfs with directIO enabled for cache files, separate disk or ZFS dataset with quota to avoid eviction. ensure fadvise settings are applied.
[14:30] Ethan Park: can you demo the verify tool quickly?
[14:33] Omar Valdez: quick demo — redwood-verify --manifest manifest.json --media /dev/sdb; returns OK and writes verify.log. It prints mismatch lines with expected vs actual checksums. note: sometimes USB serial isn't exposed depending on vendor; fallback is to log label.
[14:55] Maya Li: perfect. recap and next steps?
[15:00] Alex Kim: recap: we'll deliver transfer checklist and signed example manifest; Priya will ship runbook and stress test commands; schedule the stress test window week of 2026-03-30; customer to provide infra spec by 2026-03-22; Redwood to provide signed license within 24 business hours after CSR.
[15:18] Maya Li: that's all, thanks team.
[15:22] Alex Kim: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and calendar invite.
